claim: IDOL is widely expressed in neurons and is particularly abundant in the CA1 region of the hippocampus.
source: β-galactosidase staining of sagittal brain sections from IDOL-deficient mice revealed that IDOL was widely expressed in neurons and was particularly abundant in the CA1 region of the hippocampus (Figure 1A; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: Supported by β-galactosidase staining data shown in Figure 1A and supplementary figures, demonstrating IDOL expression pattern in brain sections.

claim: IDOL is highly expressed in neurons as confirmed by co-immunofluorescence staining of β-Gal and NeuN.
source: Co-immunofluorescence staining of β-Gal and NeuN (a neuron-specific nuclear protein) in the brain sections of Mylip+/– mice further confirmed that IDOL was highly expressed in neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data showing colocalization of β-Gal (IDOL reporter) and NeuN (neuron marker) in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: IDOL-deficient mice show striking increases in VLDLR and ApoER2 protein abundance in total cortical lysates and P2 fractions compared to wild-type mice.
source: We observed striking increases in VLDLR and ApoER2 protein abundance in total cortical lysates and P2 fractions from IDOL-deficient compared to wild-type (WT) mice (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 1B comparing protein levels between WT and IDOL-deficient mice.

claim: The induction of IDOL mRNA expression during postnatal mouse brain development between P2 and P22 correlates with decreasing ApoER2 protein despite constant Lrp8 mRNA expression.
source: We also found that the induction of mRNA encoding IDOL expression during postnatal mouse brain development between P2 and P22 correlated with decreasing ApoER2 protein despite constant Lrp8 mRNA expression (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: Supported by real-time PCR and immunoblot data in Figure 1C and D showing temporal correlation between IDOL mRNA increase and ApoER2 protein decrease.

claim: Developmental ApoER2 regulation is abolished in the absence of IDOL.
source: Moreover, this developmental ApoER2 regulation was abolished in the absence of IDOL (Figure 1D lower panel).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figure 1D showing that ApoER2 protein levels do not decrease during development in IDOL-deficient mice.

claim: The increase of IDOL expression in the post-natal period parallels that of PSD95 and the NR1 subunit of the NMDA receptor.
source: The increase of IDOL expression in the post-natal period paralleled that of PSD95 and the NR1 subunit of the NMDA receptor (Figure 1D upper panel), which rise due to the robust synaptogenesis that occurs during this time (Sans et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figure 1D and cited reference to Sans et al., 2000 regarding synaptogenesis timing.

claim: Deletion of IDOL in Mylipflox/flox neurons results in >95% reduction in IDOL mRNA and strong increases in ApoER2, VLDLR and LDLR protein.
source: Deletion of IDOL in Mylipflox/flox neurons by means of an AAV-CamKII-Cre vector resulted in >95% reduction in mRNA encoding IDOL and strong increases in ApoER2, VLDLR and LDLR protein compared to cells transduced with GFP-expressing AAV vector (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot and PCR data in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C showing effects of IDOL deletion.

claim: AAV-mediated overexpression of IDOL in primary cortical neurons greatly reduces the levels of lipoprotein receptors.
source: Conversely, AAV-mediated overexpression of IDOL in primary cortical neurons greatly reduced the levels of these lipoprotein receptors (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figure 1F showing reduced receptor levels upon IDOL overexpression.

claim: In immature neurons (DIV7), GFP-IDOL distributes widely in soma and dendritic shafts.
source: In immature neurons (7 days of in vitro culture; DIV7), GFP-IDOL distributed widely in soma and dendritic shafts (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence imaging data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A showing IDOL localization in immature neurons.

claim: In mature DIV18 neurons, GFP-IDOL concentrates at synapses and is juxtaposed with the glutamatergic presynaptic marker vGlut1.
source: However, in mature DIV18 neurons, GFP-IDOL concentrated at synapses, and was juxtaposed with the glutamatergic presynaptic marker vGlut1 (Figure 1G, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence imaging data in Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A showing colocalization with vGlut1.

claim: Synaptic enrichment of IDOL is confirmed by colocalization of PSD95 and transfected WT GFP-IDOL fusion protein in the presence of MG132.
source: This synaptic enrichment was further confirmed by colocalization of PSD95 and transfected WT GFP-IDOL fusion protein in the presence of MG132 (to block proteosomal degradation of IDOL; Figure 1H).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 1H showing colocalization with PSD95 when proteasomal degradation is blocked.

claim: Bicuculline incubation suppresses Mylip mRNA level after 2 hr and is associated with an increase in ApoER2 protein, but no change in its mRNA.
source: Bic incubation suppressed Mylip mRNA level after 2 hr, and this was associated with an increase in ApoER2 protein, but no change in its mRNA (Figure 1I,J).
evidence: Supported by real-time PCR and immunoblot data in Figure 1I and J showing effects of bicuculline treatment.

claim: Bicuculline-dependent changes in ApoER2 are abolished in neurons lacking IDOL.
source: Moreover, Bic-dependent changes in ApoER2 were abolished in neurons lacking IDOL (Figure 1J).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figure 1J comparing bicuculline effects in control and IDOL-deficient neurons.

claim: Similar results to bicuculline treatment were obtained using KCl to depolarize neurons.
source: Similar results were also obtained using KCl to depolarize neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B showing KCl effects on IDOL and ApoER2.

claim: IDOL expression results in a marked reduction in spine density in primary hippocampal neurons.
source: Primary hippocampal neurons were transduced with AAV-hSyn-GFP or AAV-hSyn-GFP-IDOL vectors at DIV 5–7, and then imaged at DIV 18–20. IDOL expression resulted in a marked reduction in spine density (Figure 2A and B)
evidence: Supported by imaging and quantification data in Figure 2A and B showing reduced spine density with IDOL overexpression.

claim: IDOL expression reduces the total and surface levels of key post-synaptic proteins including AMPAR, NMDAR1 and PSD95.
source: IDOL expression resulted in a marked reduction in spine density (Figure 2A and B) and reduced the total and surface levels of key post-synaptic proteins including AMPAR, NMDAR1 and PSD95 (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figure 2C showing reduced protein levels with IDOL overexpression.

claim: The E3 ligase activity of IDOL is required for its effects on synaptogenesis.
source: Importantly, the E3 ligase activity of IDOL was required for its effects on synaptogenesis, as expression of an inactive mutant (C387A)(Zelcer et al., 2009) failed to recapitulate these effects (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figure 2C showing that the catalytically inactive mutant does not reduce protein levels, and citation to Zelcer et al., 2009.

claim: Early IDOL overexpression markedly reduces filopodia density in DIV9-10 neurons.
source: Primary hippocampal neurons were transduced at DIV 5 and imaged at DIV 9–10, a stage at which most spines are immature and appear as long, thin filopodia. Early IDOL overexpression markedly reduced filopodia density in DIV9-10 neurons (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by imaging and quantification data in Figure 2D showing reduced filopodia density.

claim: The IDOL C387A mutant has no impact on filopodia density, indicating that E3 ligase activity is required.
source: The IDOL C387A mutant had no impact on filopodia density, indicating that E3 ligase activity was required (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by quantification data in Figure 2D comparing wild-type IDOL and C387A mutant effects.

claim: Primary hippocampal neurons that overexpressed IDOL after the major stage of spine maturation (transduced at DIV17 and imaged at DIV 21–22) do not show differences in spine density.
source: On the other hand, primary hippocampal neurons that overexpressed IDOL after the major stage of spine maturation (transduced at DIV17 and imaged at DIV 21–22) grossly did not show differences in spine density (Figure 2E)
evidence: Supported by imaging and quantification data in Figure 2E showing no change in spine density with late IDOL overexpression.

claim: Neurons overexpressing IDOL after spine maturation have comparable expression of post-synaptic proteins including AMPAR, NMDAR1 and PSD95.
source: primary hippocampal neurons that overexpressed IDOL after the major stage of spine maturation (transduced at DIV17 and imaged at DIV 21–22) grossly did not show differences in spine density (Figure 2E), and had comparable expression of post-synaptic proteins including AMPAR, NMDAR1 and PSD95 (Figure 2F)
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figure 2F showing similar protein levels with late IDOL overexpression.

claim: Excess IDOL activity affects spine formation but not maintenance.
source: primary hippocampal neurons that overexpressed IDOL after the major stage of spine maturation (transduced at DIV17 and imaged at DIV 21–22) grossly did not show differences in spine density (Figure 2E), and had comparable expression of post-synaptic proteins including AMPAR, NMDAR1 and PSD95 (Figure 2F), suggesting that excess IDOL activity affects spine formation but not maintenance.
evidence: Inferred from the differential effects of IDOL overexpression at early versus late developmental stages shown in Figures 2D-F.

claim: IDOL expression reduces the amplitude of mEPSCs but has negligible effects on their frequency.
source: The recordings of miniature excitatory postsynaptic currents (mEPSCs) at DIV 16–18 showed that IDOL expression reduced their amplitude of but had negligible effects on their frequency (Figure 3A), indicating a postsynaptic effect.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data in Figure 3A showing mEPSC amplitude and frequency measurements.

claim: The knockdown of ApoER2 using siRNA at DIV5 largely recapitulates the effects of IDOL on synaptogenesis.
source: The knockdown of ApoER2 using siRNA at DIV5 largely recapitulated the effects of IDOL on synaptogenesis (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by imaging and quantification data in Figure 3B showing similar spine density reduction with ApoER2 knockdown.

claim: Co-expression of an IDOL-resistant ApoER2 mutant (F894A) rescues the reduction in filopodia density induced by IDOL overexpression.
source: On the other hand, co-expression of an IDOL-resistant ApoER2 mutant (F894A) (Calkin et al., 2011) rescued the reduction in filopodia density induced by IDOL overexpression, while an IDOL-resistant VLDLR mutant (F832A) (Calkin et al., 2011) failed to do so (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by imaging and quantification data in Figure 3C and citations to Calkin et al., 2011 describing the mutants.

claim: An IDOL-resistant VLDLR mutant (F832A) fails to rescue the reduction in filopodia density induced by IDOL overexpression.
source: On the other hand, co-expression of an IDOL-resistant ApoER2 mutant (F894A) (Calkin et al., 2011) rescued the reduction in filopodia density induced by IDOL overexpression, while an IDOL-resistant VLDLR mutant (F832A) (Calkin et al., 2011) failed to do so (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by imaging and quantification data in Figure 3C and citations to Calkin et al., 2011.

claim: The ability of IDOL to reduce the levels of key post-synaptic proteins is preserved in Ldlr–/– neurons.
source: In addition, the ability of IDOL to reduce the levels of key post-synaptic proteins were preserved in Ldlr–/– neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A showing IDOL effects in LDLR knockout neurons.

claim: Adding neither RAP nor neutralizing antibody to Reelin abolishes the effects of IDOL on the expression of key post-synaptic proteins.
source: And adding neither RAP (a high-affinity competitive ligand for ApoE receptors) nor neutralizing antibody to Reelin (CR50) abolished the effects of IDOL on the expression of key post-synaptic proteins (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B showing IDOL effects persist with RAP or CR50 treatment.

claim: The inhibitory effects of IDOL on spinogenesis are likely mediated through ApoER2, and largely independent of the Reelin signaling pathway and the uptake of lipoprotein particles.
source: Together, these data suggested that the inhibitory effects of IDOL on spinogenesis were likely mediated through ApoER2, and largely independent of the Reelin signaling pathway and the uptake of lipoprotein particles in our experimental setting.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experimental results including rescue with IDOL-resistant ApoER2, lack of effect of RAP and CR50, and preservation of effects in LDLR knockout neurons.

claim: At DIV18-21, control neurons show numerous mature dendritic spines with typical morphology.
source: At DIV18-21, control neurons showed numerous mature dendritic spines with typical morphology (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by imaging data in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A showing spine morphology in control neurons.

claim: IDOL-deficient neurons display many filopodia-like, thin, immature spines with no enlarged spine head.
source: By contrast, IDOL-deficient neurons displayed many filopodia-like, thin, immature spines with no enlarged spine head.
evidence: Supported by imaging data described in the text and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Spine density is increased by 42% in IDOL-deficient neurons.
source: Spine density was increased by 42%, while spine head width decreased approximately 50% (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by quantification data in Figure 4A showing spine density measurements.

claim: Spine head width decreases approximately 50% in IDOL-deficient neurons.
source: Spine density was increased by 42%, while spine head width decreased approximately 50% (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by quantification data in Figure 4A showing spine head width measurements.

claim: The tips of many dendritic protrusions in IDOL-deficient neurons are not apposed to presynaptic terminals.
source: Immunostaining of IDOL-deficient neurons with the postsynaptic marker PSD95 and presynaptic marker vGluT1 further revealed that the tips of many dendritic protrusions were not apposed to presynaptic terminals (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence imaging data in Figure 4A showing lack of colocalization between dendritic protrusions and vGluT1.

claim: IDOL-deficient neurons have numerous excitatory synapses formed directly on the dendritic shafts.
source: In contrast to control neurons, in which most of the synapses were formed at the spine heads (white arrows), IDOL-deficient had numerous excitatory synapses formed directly on the dendritic shafts (red arrows) (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence imaging data in Figure 4A showing shaft synapses in IDOL-deficient neurons.

claim: IDOL is important for the proper spine morphogenesis during filopodia-to-mature spine transition process.
source: These data suggest that IDOL is important for the proper spine morphogenesis during filopodia-to-mature spine transition process.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that IDOL-deficient neurons have increased immature spines and altered synapse formation patterns.

claim: ApoER2 overexpression results in a 2-fold increase in spine density and a ~50% reduction in head width.
source: ApoER2 overexpression resulted in a 2-fold increase in spine density and a ~50% reduction in head width, largely recapitulating the effects of IDOL deficiency (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by imaging and quantification data in Figure 4B showing effects of ApoER2 overexpression.

claim: siRNA-mediated ApoER2 knockdown increases the width of spine heads in IDOL-deficient hippocampal neurons.
source: Indeed siRNA-mediated ApoER2 knockdown increased the width of spine heads in IDOL-deficient hippocampal neurons (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by imaging and quantification data in Figure 4C and immunoblot data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Precise control of synaptic ApoER2 protein levels by IDOL is critical for spine morphogenesis.
source: Thus, precise control of synaptic ApoER2 protein levels by IDOL is critical for spine morphogenesis. Either too little or too much ApoER2 leads to dysmorphic effects.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that both IDOL overexpression (reducing ApoER2) and IDOL deficiency (increasing ApoER2) lead to abnormal spine morphology.

claim: IDOL-deficient mice have higher spine density but reduced head width compared with their WT counterparts in CA1 pyramidal neurons.
source: Consistent with results from primary neuron cultures, IDOL-deficient mice had higher spine density but reduced head width compared with their WT counterparts (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by Golgi-impregnation imaging and quantification data in Figure 4D from in vivo mouse brain tissue.

claim: Deletion of IDOL from hippocampal neurons does not change total or surface levels of the GluR1 and GluR2 subunits of the AMPA receptor, nor the NR1, NR2a or NR2b subunits of NMDARs.
source: Deletion of IDOL from hippocampal neurons did not change total or surface levels of the GluR1 and GluR2 subunits of the AMPA (α-amino-3-hydrozy-5-methylisoxa-zole-4-propionic acid) receptor, nor the NR1, NR2a or NR2b subunits of NMDARs (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figure 5A showing glutamate receptor subunit levels.

claim: NR1 is appropriately localized on dendritic spines in IDOL-deficient hippocampal neurons.
source: ApoER2 has been reported to interact directly with NR1, but co-immunostaining with vGluT1 revealed that NR1 was appropriately localized on dendritic spines in IDOL-deficient hippocampal neurons (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence imaging data in Figure 5B showing NR1 localization.

claim: Total lysates and P2 fractions from the brain of 4-week-old IDOL-deficient mice show comparable levels of glutamate receptors to WT mice.
source: Consistent with these findings, total lysates and P2 fractions from the brain of 4-week-old IDOL-deficient mice showed comparable levels of glutamate receptors to WT mice (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figure 5C comparing glutamate receptor levels in WT and IDOL-deficient mice.

claim: Loss of IDOL is associated with reduced levels of the scaffold protein PSD95 in the P2 fraction.
source: However, loss of IDOL was associated with reduced levels of the scaffold protein PSD95 in the P2 fraction, possibly reflecting less scaffolding protein embedded at the postsynaptic density of the smaller spine heads observed in IDOL-deficient (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figure 5C showing PSD95 levels in P2 fractions, with inference about the mechanism.

claim: IDOL overexpression decreases the basal level of GTP-bound (active) Rac1 in primary cortical neurons.
source: We found that IDOL overexpression decreased, while IDOL knockout increased, the basal level of GTP-bound (active) Rac1 in primary cortical neurons (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by Rac1 activity assay data in Figure 5D showing GTP-bound Rac1 levels.

claim: IDOL knockout increases the basal level of GTP-bound (active) Rac1 in primary cortical neurons.
source: We found that IDOL overexpression decreased, while IDOL knockout increased, the basal level of GTP-bound (active) Rac1 in primary cortical neurons (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by Rac1 activity assay data in Figure 5D showing GTP-bound Rac1 levels.

claim: In control primary neurons, bicuculline treatment induces Rac1 activity.
source: In control primary neurons, Bic treatment induced Rac1 activity as expected (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by Rac1 activity assay data in Figure 5E showing increased GTP-bound Rac1 with bicuculline treatment.

claim: IDOL-deficient neurons show increased basal Rac1 activity, but bicuculline fails to induce, and actually reduces, Rac1 activity.
source: Interestingly, although IDOL-deficient neurons showed increased basal Rac1 activity, Bic failed to induce, and actually reduced, Rac1 activity (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by Rac1 activity assay data in Figure 5E comparing basal and bicuculline-stimulated conditions.

claim: Induction of ERK phosphorylation in response to bicuculline treatment is not impaired by either IDOL knockdown or overexpression.
source: However, induction of ERK phosphorylation in response to Bic treatment was not impaired by either IDOL knockdown or overexpression (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figure 5E showing ERK phosphorylation levels.

claim: The IDOL-ApoER2 axis selectively affects signaling pathways related to actin remodeling.
source: This observation suggests that the IDOL-ApoER2 axis selectively affects signaling pathways related to actin remodeling.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that IDOL affects Rac1 activity but not ERK phosphorylation in response to neuronal activity.

claim: Neurons overexpressing ApoER2 show increased basal Rac1 activity and compromised Rac1 induction upon bicuculline treatment.
source: Supporting the notion that ApoER2 is the principle mediator of IDOL effects on Rac1, the Rac1 activity phenotype of neurons overexpressing ApoER2 resembled that of IDOL-deficient neurons (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A): both showed increased basal Rac1 activity and compromised Rac1 induction upon Bic treatment.
evidence: Supported by Rac1 activity assay data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A showing similar phenotypes.

claim: Loss of IDOL increases protein levels of JIP1 in both total brain lysates and P2 fractions.
source: We found that loss of IDOL increased protein levels of JIP1 in both total brain lysates and P2 fractions (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B showing JIP1 protein levels.

claim: Loss of IDOL does not affect protein levels of Tiam1.
source: Consistent with this idea, loss of IDOL did not affect protein levels of Tiam1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C showing Tiam1 protein levels.

claim: Loss of IDOL markedly alters Tiam1 localization in primary neurons.
source: loss of IDOL did not affect protein levels of Tiam1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), but markedly altered its localization in primary neurons (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence imaging data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D showing Tiam1 localization.

claim: In WT neurons Tiam1 is enriched within the spine heads.
source: In WT neurons Tiam1 was enriched within the spine heads as expected, but it was mislocalized to the base of the spines in IDOL-deficient neurons.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence imaging data described in the text and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Tiam1 is mislocalized to the base of the spines in IDOL-deficient neurons.
source: In WT neurons Tiam1 was enriched within the spine heads as expected, but it was mislocalized to the base of the spines in IDOL-deficient neurons.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence imaging data described in the text and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Changes in JIP1 and Tiam1 may contribute to the decoupling between NMDAR and Rac1 observed in the absence of IDOL.
source: These observations suggest that changes in JIP1 and Tiam1 may contribute to the decoupling between NMDAR and Rac1 observed in the absence of IDOL.
evidence: Inferred from the observed changes in JIP1 levels and Tiam1 localization in IDOL-deficient neurons, combined with the known roles of these proteins in NMDAR-Rac1 coupling.

claim: Glycine treatment increases ApoER2 protein in hippocampal neurons after 40 min.
source: Consistent with our prior findings that neuronal activity determined ApoER2 protein levels, we found that glycine treatment increased ApoER2 protein in hippocampal neurons after 40 min, and that this effect was entirely dependent on IDOL expression (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figure 6A showing ApoER2 protein levels after glycine treatment.

claim: The glycine-induced increase in ApoER2 protein is entirely dependent on IDOL expression.
source: Consistent with our prior findings that neuronal activity determined ApoER2 protein levels, we found that glycine treatment increased ApoER2 protein in hippocampal neurons after 40 min, and that this effect was entirely dependent on IDOL expression (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figure 6A comparing glycine effects in control and IDOL-deficient neurons.

claim: Basal mEPSCs recordings of hippocampal neurons do not reveal changes in either amplitude or frequency of mEPSCs upon IDOL deletion.
source: Basal mEPSCs recordings of hippocampal neurons did not reveal changes in either amplitude or frequency of mEPSCs upon IDOL deletion (Figure 6B), suggesting that although loss of IDOL affects spine morphogenesis, it does not have a major detrimental impact on basal synaptic transmission.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data in Figure 6B showing mEPSC measurements in basal conditions.

claim: Loss of IDOL affects spine morphogenesis but does not have a major detrimental impact on basal synaptic transmission.
source: Basal mEPSCs recordings of hippocampal neurons did not reveal changes in either amplitude or frequency of mEPSCs upon IDOL deletion (Figure 6B), suggesting that although loss of IDOL affects spine morphogenesis, it does not have a major detrimental impact on basal synaptic transmission.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that IDOL deletion causes morphological changes but does not alter basal mEPSCs.

claim: The amplitude and frequency of mEPSCs are increased in GFP-expressing hippocampal neurons after stimulation with glycine.
source: The amplitude and frequency of mEPSCs were increased in GFP-expressing hippocampal neurons after stimulation with glycine as expected.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data described in the text and shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Glycine stimulation does not produce increased mEPSCs in IDOL-deficient neurons, suggesting a defect in LTP.
source: By contrast, glycine stimulation did not produce increased mEPSCs in IDOL-deficient neurons, suggesting a defect in LTP (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data in Figure 6B comparing glycine effects in control and IDOL-deficient neurons.

claim: Glycine treatment induces phosphorylation of ERK and GluR1 (S845) to a similar extent in WT and IDOL-deficient neurons.
source: The failure to enhance mEPSCs upon glycine treatment was unlikely to be due to a complete block in NMDAR activation, as glycine treatment induced phosphorylation of ERK and GluR1 (S845) to a similar extent in WT and IDOL-deficient neurons (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 showing phosphorylation levels.

claim: Glycine treatment causes a 42% increase in spine number in WT neurons.
source: Glycine treatment caused a 42% increase in spine number in WT neurons (Figure 6C and D), and we observed more spines with head width >0.8 μM (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by imaging and quantification data in Figure 6C and D showing spine density changes.

claim: Glycine treatment increases the number of spines with head width >0.8 μM in WT neurons.
source: Glycine treatment caused a 42% increase in spine number in WT neurons (Figure 6C and D), and we observed more spines with head width >0.8 μM (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by quantification data in Figure 6D showing spine head width measurements.

claim: Glycine treatment fails to increase either spine number or head width in IDOL-deficient neurons.
source: By contrast, glycine treatment failed to increase either spine number or head width in IDOL-deficient neurons (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by quantification data in Figure 6D comparing glycine effects in control and IDOL-deficient neurons.

claim: Defects in spine structural remodeling upon NMDAR activation may underlie the failure to induce LTP in the absence of IDOL.
source: These findings suggest that defects in spine structural remodeling upon NMDAR activation may underlie the failure to induce LTP in the absence of IDOL.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that IDOL-deficient neurons fail to show both structural spine changes and functional LTP in response to glycine treatment.

claim: There is no difference in the input-output curves between WT and IDOL-deficient hippocampal slices.
source: We found no difference in the IO curves between WT and IDOL-deficient slices (Figure 6E), suggesting that basal synaptic function was not affected by the absence of IDOL.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data in Figure 6E showing input-output relationships.

claim: Basal synaptic function is not affected by the absence of IDOL in hippocampal slices.
source: We found no difference in the IO curves between WT and IDOL-deficient slices (Figure 6E), suggesting that basal synaptic function was not affected by the absence of IDOL.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that input-output curves are similar in WT and IDOL-deficient slices.

claim: High frequency stimulation of Schaffer collateral synapses causes a robust increase in the slope of the fEPSPs that persists throughout the 1 hr recording period after HFS in both WT and IDOL-deficient slices.
source: In both WT and IDOL-deficient slices, a standard protocol of high frequency stimulation (HFS) of Schaeffer collateral synapses caused a robust increase in the slope of the fEPSPs that persisted throughout the 1 hr recording period after HFS (Figure 6F).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data in Figure 6F showing fEPSP slopes over time.

claim: The magnitude of LTP remains at a persistently high level in WT slices for the duration of the recording.
source: However, whereas the magnitude of LTP remained at a persistently high level in WT slices for the duration of the recording, in IDOL-deficient slices the magnitude of LTP gradually decreased over time
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data described in the text and shown in Figure 6F.

claim: In IDOL-deficient slices the magnitude of LTP gradually decreases over time such that by the end of the recording, the potentiation in the slope of the fEPSPs is markedly reduced compared to WT mice.
source: However, whereas the magnitude of LTP remained at a persistently high level in WT slices for the duration of the recording, in IDOL-deficient slices the magnitude of LTP gradually decreased over time such that, by the end of the recording, the potentiation in the slope of the fEPSPs was markedly reduced compared to WT mice (Figure 6F; 186.1 ± 6.4% in WT vs. 133.0 ± 2.5% in IDOL KO, p=0.00654, Mann-Whitney U-test).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data in Figure 6F showing quantified LTP magnitude at 55-60 minutes.

claim: There is no significant difference in the cortical map size for D2W at baseline between WT and IDOL-deficient groups.
source: There was no significant difference in the cortical map size for D2W at baseline between WT (N = 7) and IDOL-deficient (N = 8) groups (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by optical intrinsic signal imaging data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B showing baseline map sizes.

claim: In WT mice, there is an increase in the size of the functional representation of the spared D2 whisker relative to the pre-deprivation baseline beginning at 7 days after whisker plucking and persisting throughout the imaging period.
source: In WT mice, we observed an increase in the size of the functional representation of the spared D2 whisker relative to the pre-deprivation baseline beginning at 7 days after whisker plucking and persisting throughout the imaging period (Figure 7B and C).
evidence: Supported by optical intrinsic signal imaging data in Figure 7B and C showing map size changes over time.

claim: There is no increase in the area of the functional D2W representation in IDOL-deficient mice at any time after whisker deprivation.
source: By contrast, there was no increase in the area of the functional D2W representation in IDOL-deficient mice at any time after whisker deprivation (Figure 7B and C).
evidence: Supported by optical intrinsic signal imaging data in Figure 7B and C showing lack of map expansion in IDOL-deficient mice.

claim: There is a significantly larger D2W map size in WT mice compared to IDOL-deficient mice after whisker plucking.
source: When comparing the two genotypes, we observed a significantly larger D2W map size in WT mice after whisker plucking (Two-way ANOVA with repeated measures, interaction between genotype and time p=0.004).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of optical intrinsic signal imaging data comparing WT and IDOL-deficient mice.

claim: At +21 days after whisker deprivation, there is a +50% change in D2W map size from baseline in WT compared to no change in IDOL-deficient mice.
source: This difference was most noticeable at +21 d, which coincides with the time when previous studies have detected the largest effect of whisker deprivation on OIS map size (Margolis et al., 2012). We found a + 50% change in map size from baseline in WT compared to no change in IDOL-deficient mice (Figure 7D).
evidence: Supported by quantification data in Figure 7D and citation to Margolis et al., 2012 regarding timing of maximal effects.

claim: Whisker deprivation does not affect the cortical hind limb (HL) map in WT control mice or in IDOL-deficient mice.
source: In control experiments, we found that whisker deprivation did not affect the cortical hind limb (HL) map in WT control mice or in IDOL-deficient mice (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: Supported by optical intrinsic signal imaging data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C and D showing stable HL maps.

claim: IDOL plays an indispensable role in the experience-dependent plasticity of neural circuits in vivo.
source: These findings demonstrate that IDOL plays an indispensable role in the experience-dependent plasticity of neural circuits in vivo.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that IDOL-deficient mice completely fail to show experience-dependent reorganization of cortical maps.

claim: WT mice perform better than IDOL-deficient mice in the Morris water maze task, as measured by reduced escape latencies over the course of the training trials.
source: WT mice performed better than IDOL-deficient mice in this task, as measured by reduced escape latencies over the course of the training trials, although both groups improved (Figure 8A).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 8A showing escape latencies during training.

claim: WT mice spend significantly more time in the target quadrant after 7 or 9 days training in the Morris water maze probe trial.
source: WT mice spent significantly more time in the target quadrant after 7 or 9 days training, while IDOL-deficient mice showed no improvement (Figure 8B).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 8B showing time spent in target quadrant during probe trials.

claim: IDOL-deficient mice show no improvement in time spent in the target quadrant after training in the Morris water maze.
source: WT mice spent significantly more time in the target quadrant after 7 or 9 days training, while IDOL-deficient mice showed no improvement (Figure 8B).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 8B showing lack of improvement in IDOL-deficient mice.

claim: IDOL-deficient mice fail to acquire the memory for the location of the hidden platform in the Morris water maze.
source: This finding suggested that IDOL-deficient mice failed to acquire the memory for the location of the hidden platform.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that IDOL-deficient mice do not show increased time in the target quadrant during probe trials.

claim: Both WT and IDOL-deficient mice perform similarly in the visible platform test of the Morris water maze.
source: These performance differences could not be attributed to vision or locomotor defects, as both groups performed similarly in the visible platform test (Figure 8C), and exhibited comparable swimming speed (Figure 8D).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 8C showing escape latencies for visible platform.

claim: WT and IDOL-deficient mice exhibit comparable swimming speed in the Morris water maze.
source: These performance differences could not be attributed to vision or locomotor defects, as both groups performed similarly in the visible platform test (Figure 8C), and exhibited comparable swimming speed (Figure 8D).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 8D showing swimming speed measurements.

claim: IDOL-deficient mice spend less time freezing than WT mice in contextual fear conditioning, indicating a failure to associate the foot-shock with the context.
source: IDOL-deficient mice spent less time freezing than WT mice, indicating a failure to associate the foot-shock with the context (Figure 8E).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 8E showing freezing time measurements.

claim: Stereotactic injection of AVV-IDOL into the hippocampus of C57Bl/6 mice is associated with decreased performance in the fear-conditioning test compared to mice injected with AAV-GFP control virus.
source: Stereotactic injection of AVV-IDOL into the hippocampus of C57Bl/6 mice (Figure 8F) was associated with decreased performance in the fear-conditioning test compared to mice injected with AAV-GFP control virus (Figure 8G).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 8G showing freezing time in AAV-IDOL versus AAV-GFP injected mice.

claim: Excess IDOL expression in hippocampus impairs learning and memory.
source: The finding that excess IDOL expression in hippocampus impairs learning and memory is consistent with prior studies showing that loss of ApoER2 impairs these processes (Weeber et al., 2002).
evidence: Inferred from the behavioral data showing impaired fear conditioning with IDOL overexpression, and cited reference to Weeber et al., 2002.

claim: Loss of ApoER2 impairs learning and memory processes.
source: The finding that excess IDOL expression in hippocampus impairs learning and memory is consistent with prior studies showing that loss of ApoER2 impairs these processes (Weeber et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Weeber et al., 2002.

claim: Precise controls of ApoER2 protein levels are important for normal brain function.
source: The finding that loss of IDOL also impairs learning and memory strongly reinforces the conclusion that precise controls of ApoER2 protein levels are important for normal brain function. Either too little or too much ApoER2 is detrimental.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that both IDOL deficiency (high ApoER2) and IDOL overexpression (low ApoER2) impair learning and memory.

claim: The IDOL-ApoER2 axis is a key player in regulating dendritic spine initiation and morphogenesis and their structural remodeling downstream of glutamate receptor activation.
source: Our data implicate the IDOL-ApoER2 axis as a key player in regulating dendritic spine initiation and morphogenesis and their structural remodeling downstream of glutamate receptor activation.
evidence: Inferred from the multiple experimental findings showing IDOL-ApoER2 effects on spine formation, maturation, and activity-dependent remodeling.

claim: Loss of IDOL does not globally disrupt CNS development or basal synaptic transmission.
source: Loss of IDOL does not globally disrupt CNS development or basal synaptic transmission, but greatly impairs the functional plasticity of synapses and neural circuits in vivo.
evidence: Supported by data showing normal basal synaptic function but impaired plasticity in IDOL-deficient neurons and mice.

claim: Loss of IDOL greatly impairs the functional plasticity of synapses and neural circuits in vivo.
source: Loss of IDOL does not globally disrupt CNS development or basal synaptic transmission, but greatly impairs the functional plasticity of synapses and neural circuits in vivo.
evidence: Supported by data showing impaired LTP, defective structural remodeling, and failed experience-dependent plasticity in IDOL-deficient neurons and mice.

claim: IDOL-deficient neurons are defective in their ability to undergo activity-dependent spine remodeling.
source: IDOL-deficient neurons are defective in their ability to undergo activity-dependent spine remodeling and IDOL-deficient mice show impaired cognitive function and a complete failure to reorganize neural circuits.
evidence: Supported by data showing lack of spine structural changes in response to glycine treatment in IDOL-deficient neurons.

claim: IDOL-deficient mice show impaired cognitive function.
source: IDOL-deficient neurons are defective in their ability to undergo activity-dependent spine remodeling and IDOL-deficient mice show impaired cognitive function and a complete failure to reorganize neural circuits.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data showing impaired performance in Morris water maze and fear conditioning tests.

claim: IDOL-deficient mice show a complete failure to reorganize neural circuits.
source: IDOL-deficient neurons are defective in their ability to undergo activity-dependent spine remodeling and IDOL-deficient mice show impaired cognitive function and a complete failure to reorganize neural circuits.
evidence: Supported by optical intrinsic signal imaging data showing no expansion of cortical maps after whisker deprivation.

claim: Loss of ApoER2 impairs LTP.
source: Since loss of ApoER2 impairs LTP, and since ApoER2 mediates Reelin signaling to enhance learning and memory in mice (Bosch et al., 2016; Niu et al., 2008; Rogers et al., 2011), it has been suggested that increased ApoER2 expression would be beneficial.
evidence: Supported by citations to Bosch et al., 2016; Niu et al., 2008; Rogers et al., 2011.

claim: ApoER2 mediates Reelin signaling to enhance learning and memory in mice.
source: Since loss of ApoER2 impairs LTP, and since ApoER2 mediates Reelin signaling to enhance learning and memory in mice (Bosch et al., 2016; Niu et al., 2008; Rogers et al., 2011), it has been suggested that increased ApoER2 expression would be beneficial.
evidence: Supported by citations to Bosch et al., 2016; Niu et al., 2008; Rogers et al., 2011.

claim: The constitutive ApoER2 expression caused by IDOL deficiency is detrimental to proper dendritic spine morphogenesis and the plasticity of neural circuits.
source: On the contrary, we have shown here that the constitutive ApoER2 expression caused by IDOL deficiency is detrimental to proper dendritic spine morphogenesis and the plasticity of neural circuits.
evidence: Supported by data showing abnormal spine morphology, impaired LTP, and failed circuit reorganization in IDOL-deficient neurons and mice.

claim: ApoER2 protein expression in mature neurons is acutely regulated at the post-translational level in response to neuronal activity and the induction of LTP.
source: Furthermore, we found that ApoER2 protein expression in mature neurons is not constant, but is acutely regulated at the post-translational level in response to neuronal activity and the induction of LTP.
evidence: Supported by data showing changes in ApoER2 protein levels in response to bicuculline and glycine treatment without changes in mRNA levels.

claim: IDOL provides a mechanism to actively control ApoER2 levels in order to facilitate the development of new spines and synapses.
source: IDOL thus provides a mechanism to actively control ApoER2 levels in order to facilitate the development of new spines and synapses.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that IDOL regulates ApoER2 levels in response to activity and that this regulation is important for spine formation and plasticity.

claim: Spine density is decreased in ApoER2 KO mice.
source: Our observation that IDOL bidirectionally regulate spine density through ApoER2 is consistent with previous studies showing that spine density is decreased in ApoER2 KO mice and increased in the setting of ApoER2 overexpression (Dumanis et al., 2011; Wasser et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dumanis et al., 2011; Wasser et al., 2014.

claim: Spine density is increased in the setting of ApoER2 overexpression.
source: Our observation that IDOL bidirectionally regulate spine density through ApoER2 is consistent with previous studies showing that spine density is decreased in ApoER2 KO mice and increased in the setting of ApoER2 overexpression (Dumanis et al., 2011; Wasser et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dumanis et al., 2011; Wasser et al., 2014.

claim: Lrp8 lacking exon 16 increases the stability of ApoER2 in neurons and is associated with higher spine density.
source: Lrp8 lacking exon 16, which encodes the O-linked sugar (OLS) domain, increased the stability of ApoER2 in neurons and was associated with higher spine density (Wasser et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wasser et al., 2014.

claim: Mild increases in ApoER2 levels in response to exon 16 deletion lead to enhanced LTP.
source: Interestingly, while mild increases in ApoER2 levels in response to exon 16 deletion led to enhanced LTP (Wasser et al., 2014), we showed constitutive high level of ApoER2 expression in IDOL-deficient mice severely impaired LTP.
evidence: Supported by citation to Wasser et al., 2014.

claim: The dynamic regulation of ApoER2 levels, rather than its absolute abundance, is critical for the functional plasticity of spine synapses.
source: To reconcile these observations, we propose that the dynamic regulation of ApoER2 levels, rather than its absolute abundance, is critical for the functional plasticity of spine synapses.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that mild stable increases in ApoER2 enhance LTP while constitutive high levels impair LTP, suggesting the importance of regulation rather than absolute levels.

claim: ApoER2 lacking the OLS domain is likely still regulated by IDOL in response to neuronal activity.
source: ApoER2 lacking the OLS domain is likely still regulated by IDOL in response to neuronal activity, although its dynamics will be based on the higher ApoER2 level.
evidence: Inferred from the understanding that exon 16 deletion affects stability but not IDOL-mediated regulation, combined with knowledge of IDOL's mechanism of action.

claim: Loss of IDOL completely abolishes activity-dependent regulation of ApoER2 levels.
source: On the contrary, loss of IDOL completely abolished activity-dependent regulation of ApoER2 levels, which consequently led to impaired structural and functional plasticity of dendritic spines.
evidence: Supported by data showing that bicuculline-induced changes in ApoER2 are abolished in IDOL-deficient neurons.

claim: Rac signaling may be involved in the regulation of neuronal structural plasticity by ApoER2.
source: Our study also suggests that Rac signaling may be involved in the regulation of neuronal structural plasticity by ApoER2.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that IDOL-ApoER2 axis affects Rac1 activity and that Rac1 is known to regulate spine morphology.

claim: Spatial and temporal coordination of actin dynamics are prerequisite for synapse formation and plasticity.
source: Considerable evidence suggests that spatial and temporal coordination of actin dynamics are prerequisite for synapse formation and plasticity (Dillon and Goda, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dillon and Goda, 2005.

claim: Rho small GTPases (particularly RhoA, Rac1, Cdc42) are regulators of the actin cytoskeleton that have a profound influence on spine morphogenesis.
source: The Rho small GTPases (particularly RhoA, Rac1, Cdc42) are regulators of the actin cytoskeleton that have a profound influence on spine morphogenesis (Luo, 2002; Newey et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Luo, 2002; Newey et al., 2005.

claim: Tiam1 is responsible for the coupling between NMDAR and Rac1.
source: One Rac-GEF implicated in the activity-dependent remodeling of dendritic arbors is Tiam1, which is responsible for the coupling between NMDAR and Rac1 (Tolias et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tolias et al., 2005.

claim: The bidirectional regulation of Rac1 activity by IDOL aligns closely with IDOL's impact on spine morphogenesis.
source: The bidirectional regulation of Rac1 activity by IDOL aligns closely with IDOL's impact on spine morphogenesis.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that IDOL overexpression reduces both Rac1 activity and spine density, while IDOL deficiency increases both.

claim: ApoER2 may be a component of a 'signaling hub' modulating Rac1 activity and actin remodeling of dendritic spines.
source: We speculate that ApoER2 may be component of a 'signaling hub' modulating Rac1 activity and actin remodeling of dendritic spines.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on the observed effects of ApoER2 on multiple signaling components including Rac1, JIP1, and Tiam1.

claim: JIP is localized at post-synaptic densities (PSD) in neurons.
source: Recent studies have shown that JIP is localized at post-synaptic densities (PSD) in neurons, and is indispensable for the normal function of NMDA receptors (Kennedy et al., 2007; Pellet et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kennedy et al., 2007; Pellet et al., 2000.

claim: JIP is indispensable for the normal function of NMDA receptors.
source: Recent studies have shown that JIP is localized at post-synaptic densities (PSD) in neurons, and is indispensable for the normal function of NMDA receptors (Kennedy et al., 2007; Pellet et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kennedy et al., 2007; Pellet et al., 2000.

claim: Postsynaptic JIP and Tiam1 could be involved in mediating the effects of IDOL-ApoER2 axis on Rac1 activity.
source: Our data suggest that postsynaptic JIP (Stockinger et al., 2000; Verhey et al., 2001) and Tiam1 (Buchsbaum et al., 2002) could be involved in mediating the effects of IDOL-ApoER2 axis on Rac1 activity.
evidence: Inferred from the observed changes in JIP1 levels and Tiam1 localization in IDOL-deficient neurons, supported by citations to Stockinger et al., 2000; Verhey et al., 2001; Buchsbaum et al., 2002.

claim: JIP1 is an important regulator of axonal development and growth.
source: However, since JIP1 is also an important regulator of axonal development and growth (Dajas-Bailador et al., 2008), distinguishing the pre- and post-synaptic functions of JIP1 is technically challenging.
evidence: Supported by citation to Dajas-Bailador et al., 2008.

claim: The IDOL-dependent changes in ApoER2 abundance modulate dendritic filopodia initiation and synapse maturation.
source: IDOL-dependent changes in ApoER2 abundance modulate dendritic filopodia initiation and synapse maturation.
evidence: Supported by data showing effects of IDOL manipulation on filopodia density and spine maturation.

claim: Control of lipoprotein receptor abundance by IDOL is a post-transcriptional mechanism underlying the structural and functional plasticity of synapses and neural circuits.
source: These results identify control of lipoprotein receptor abundance by IDOL as a post-transcriptional mechanism underlying the structural and functional plasticity of synapses and neural circuits.
evidence: Inferred from the comprehensive data showing IDOL regulates ApoER2 protein levels (not mRNA) and that this regulation is critical for spine plasticity and circuit reorganization.

claim: Learning and memory are associated with long-term structural changes at synapses.
source: Learning and memory are associated with long-term structural changes at synapses (Lamprecht and LeDoux, 2004)
evidence: Supported by citation to Lamprecht and LeDoux, 2004.

claim: There is a direct relationship between spine morphology and synaptic function.
source: there is a direct relationship between spine morphology and synaptic function (Dillon and Goda, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dillon and Goda, 2005.

claim: Spines with large heads express higher levels of AMPA receptors and establish stronger synaptic connections.
source: Spines with large heads express higher levels of AMPA receptors and establish stronger synaptic connections (Tada and Sheng, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tada and Sheng, 2006.

claim: Synaptic plasticity and learning are associated with changes in spine morphology that depend on NMDAR activation.
source: In addition, mounting evidence indicates that synaptic plasticity and learning are associated with changes in spine morphology and that these morphological changes depend on NMDAR activation (Gambino et al., 2014; Hayashi-Takagi et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gambino et al., 2014; Hayashi-Takagi et al., 2015.

claim: LTP-inducing stimuli cause the formation of new spines and the enlargement of existing ones.
source: LTP-inducing stimuli cause the formation of new spines and the enlargement of existing ones (Matsuzaki et al., 2004; Nägerl et al., 2004)
evidence: Supported by citations to Matsuzaki et al., 2004; Nägerl et al., 2004.

claim: LTD is associated with the shrinkage and elimination of spines.
source: whereas LTD is associated with the shrinkage and elimination of spines (Okamoto et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Okamoto et al., 2004.

claim: Spine morphogenesis and remodeling provide a physical basis for memory in neural networks.
source: Thus, spine morphogenesis and remodeling provide a physical basis for memory in neural networks (Kasai et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kasai et al., 2003.

claim: ApoE receptors are members of the low-density lipoprotein receptor gene family that play important roles in maintaining the proper function of neurons.
source: ApoE receptors are members of the low-density lipoprotein receptor gene family that play important roles in maintaining the proper function of neurons (Herz and Bock, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Herz and Bock, 2002.

claim: ApoER2 and VLDLR bind Reelin in addition to ApoE.
source: ApoE Receptor 2 (ApoER2/LRP8) and the very low-density lipoprotein receptor (VLDLR) bind Reelin in addition to ApoE
evidence: Supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: ApoER2/VLDLR-mediated Reelin signaling is essential for controlling neuronal migration and positioning during early brain development.
source: and ApoER2/VLDLR-mediated Reelin signaling is essential for controlling neuronal migration and positioning during early brain development (Herz and Chen, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Herz and Chen, 2006.

claim: ApoER2 is required for the maintenance of proper synaptic function in adulthood.
source: ApoER2 is also required for the maintenance of proper synaptic function in adulthood (D'Arcangelo, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to D'Arcangelo, 2005.

claim: Mice lacking ApoER2 display a defect in LTP while exhibiting normal baseline synaptic transmission.
source: Mice lacking ApoER2 display a defect in LTP while exhibiting normal baseline synaptic transmission (Weeber et al., 2002), suggesting a role for ApoER2 in synaptic plasticity.
evidence: Supported by citation to Weeber et al., 2002.

claim: Long-term synaptic plasticity requires activity-dependent modifications of synaptic strength and connections.
source: Long-term synaptic plasticity requires activity-dependent modifications of synaptic strength and connections.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: Long-term synaptic plasticity involves changes in glutamate receptor trafficking, cytoskeleton remodeling, and proteasome-mediated local protein degradation.
source: This spatially and temporally coordinated process involves multiple components, including changes in glutamate receptor trafficking, cytoskeleton remodeling, and proteasome-mediated local protein degradation (Mabb and Ehlers, 2010; Murakoshi and Yasuda, 2012; Shepherd and Huganir, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mabb and Ehlers, 2010; Murakoshi and Yasuda, 2012; Shepherd and Huganir, 2007.

claim: IDOL is an E3 ubiquitin ligase whose expression is transcriptionally controlled by liver X receptors (LXRs) in cell types such as hepatocytes and macrophages.
source: One candidate physiological regulator of ApoER2 signaling is Inducible Degrader of the LDL receptor (IDOL; encoded by the Mylip gene), an E3 ubiquitin ligase whose expression is transcriptionally controlled by liver X receptors in (LXRs) in cell types such as hepatocytes and macrophages (Zelcer et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zelcer et al., 2009.

claim: The IDOL-UBE2D complex ubiquitinates the LDLR on its cytoplasmic domain, thereby targeting it for lysosomal degradation.
source: The IDOL-UBE2D complex ubiquitinates the LDLR on its cytoplasmic domain, thereby targeting it for lysosomal degradation (Zhang et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2011.

claim: The LXR-IDOL pathway regulates cellular cholesterol levels and impacts plasma LDL levels in primates.
source: Prior studies have shown that the LXR-IDOL pathway regulates cellular cholesterol levels and impacts plasma LDL levels in primates (Hong et al., 2014; Scotti et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hong et al., 2014; Scotti et al., 2011.

claim: Studies in cultured cells have shown that IDOL promotes the degradation of ApoER2 and VLDLR.
source: Studies in cultured cells have shown that IDOL also promotes the degradation of ApoER2 and VLDLR (Hong et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citation to Hong et al., 2010.

claim: IDOL and LXR signaling regulate lipoprotein receptors in a cell type-specific manner.
source: Furthermore, since IDOL and LXR signaling regulate lipoprotein receptors in a cell type-specific manner (Hong et al., 2014), the potential impact of IDOL and LXR on neuronal ApoE receptor biology and neuronal physiology cannot yet be predicted.
evidence: Supported by citation to Hong et al., 2014.

claim: The early postnatal stage is a critical period of spine elaboration, development and maturation.
source: The early postnatal stage is a critical period of spine elaboration, development and maturation (Yuste and Bonhoeffer, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yuste and Bonhoeffer, 2004.

claim: Mature spines are characterized by bulbous heads that are connected to the dendritic shafts by narrow necks.
source: Mature spines are characterized by bulbous heads that are connected to the dendritic shafts by narrow necks (Hering and Sheng, 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hering and Sheng, 2001.

claim: The induction of Rac1 activity downstream of glutamate receptors, particularly NMDAR, plays a central role in promoting actin polymerization and enlargement of the spine head.
source: The induction of Rac1 activity downstream of glutamate receptors, particularly NMDAR, plays a central role in promoting actin polymerization and enlargement of the spine head (Xie et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Xie et al., 2007.

claim: JIP1/2 interact with ApoER2.
source: It has previously been reported that c-jun-terminal kinase interacting proteins 1/2 (JIP1/2) interact with ApoER2 (Stockinger et al., 2000)
evidence: Supported by citation to Stockinger et al., 2000.

claim: JIP1/2 interact with Tiam1.
source: It has previously been reported that c-jun-terminal kinase interacting proteins 1/2 (JIP1/2) interact with ApoER2 (Stockinger et al., 2000) as well as Tiam1 (Buchsbaum et al., 2002)
evidence: Supported by citation to Buchsbaum et al., 2002.

claim: Brief stimulation of postsynaptic NMDAR induces rapid insertion and clustering of AMPA receptors at synapses and consequently enhanced mEPSCs.
source: Brief stimulation of postsynaptic NMDAR induces rapid insertion and clustering of AMPA receptors at synapses and consequently enhanced mEPSCs (Lu et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lu et al., 2001.

claim: Alteration of dendritic spine morphology and density in response to neuronal activity is a vital component of neural plasticity.
source: Alteration of dendritic spine morphology and density in response to neuronal activity is a vital component of neural plasticity (Hotulainen and Hoogenraad, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hotulainen and Hoogenraad, 2010.

claim: The IDOL-ApoER2 pathway helps to balance the mobility and stability of dendritic spines, and modulates the speed of spine maturation and synapse formation.
source: We speculate that the IDOL-ApoER2 pathway helps to balance the mobility and stability of dendritic spines, and modulates the speed of spine maturation and synapse formation.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on the observed effects of IDOL-ApoER2 on spine morphology and maturation.

claim: High ApoER2 levels during the early postnatal period may serve to keep spines immature and motile.
source: High ApoER2 levels during the early postnatal period may serve to keep spines immature and motile.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on the observation that IDOL deficiency (high ApoER2) leads to immature spine morphology.

claim: Spine motility permits the sampling of large numbers of potential presynaptic partners before connections are stabilized via activity-dependent mechanisms.
source: This would be advantageous, because spine motility permits the sampling of large numbers of potential presynaptic partners before connections are stabilized via activity-dependent mechanisms (Jontes and Smith, 2000; Portera-Cailliau et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jontes and Smith, 2000; Portera-Cailliau et al., 2003.

claim: The IDOL-ApoER2 pathway may function as a negative feedback mechanism similar to homeostatic scaling for the maintenance of neuronal network stability.
source: We further hypothesize that the IDOL-ApoER2 pathway may function as a negative feedback mechanism similar to homeostatic scaling for the maintenance of neuronal network stability.
evidence: Speculative hypothesis based on the observed effects of IDOL-ApoER2 on activity-dependent plasticity.

claim: Hebbian plasticity, including LTP and LTD, provoke positive feedback responses and are potentially prone to instability.
source: Hebbian plasticity, including LTP and LTD, provoke positive feedback responses and are potentially prone to instability (Turrigiano, 2008; Vitureira and Goda, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Turrigiano, 2008; Vitureira and Goda, 2013.

claim: In mature neurons, IDOL expression is suppressed by glutamate receptor activity, leading to the stabilization of ApoER2.
source: In mature neurons, IDOL expression is suppressed by glutamate receptor activity, leading to the stabilization of ApoER2.
evidence: Supported by data showing bicuculline treatment suppresses IDOL mRNA and increases ApoER2 protein.

claim: Increased ApoER2 expression above a certain threshold would uncouple activity-induced Rac1 induction and actin polymerization, thus preventing the further enhancement of LTP.
source: Once it passes a certain threshold, this increased ApoER2 expression would be predicted to uncouple activity-induced Rac1 induction and actin polymerization, thus preventing the further enhancement of LTP.
evidence: Speculative prediction based on the observed decoupling of NMDAR and Rac1 in IDOL-deficient neurons with high ApoER2 levels.

claim: ApoER2 is concentrated in the P2 cellular fraction, which includes postsynaptic densities.
source: ApoER2 has been reported to be concentrated in the P2 cellular fraction, which includes postsynaptic densities (Beffert et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Beffert et al., 2005.

claim: PSD95 and the NR1 subunit of the NMDA receptor rise due to the robust synaptogenesis that occurs during the early postnatal period.
source: The increase of IDOL expression in the post-natal period paralleled that of PSD95 and the NR1 subunit of the NMDA receptor (Figure 1D upper panel), which rise due to the robust synaptogenesis that occurs during this time (Sans et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sans et al., 2000.
